What is hybrid search in RAG, and why co: Hybrid search runs both a sparse keyword-based retriever (BM25, matching exact terms) and a dense vector similarity search (matching semantic meaning) in parallel, then merges/re-ranks the combined results. Vector search alone can miss exact-match needs (a specific error code, product SKU, or acronym that has no strong semantic embedding neighbor), while BM25 alone misses paraphrased or conceptually-related queries with no shared vocabulary - combining both covers the failure modes each has individually, which is why most production RAG systems use hybrid retrieval rather than pure vector search.
How would you handle multi-hop questions: A single retrieval pass often fails multi-hop questions since the query embedding doesn't clearly point to either intermediate fact needed. Handle this with iterative/agentic retrieval - have the LLM issue an initial retrieval, reason about what's still missing, generate a follow-up query for the next piece of information, and repeat until it has enough to answer (this is effectively 'agentic RAG') - rather than a single fixed retrieve-then-generate pass that assumes one retrieval step is always sufficient.
What is query rewriting/query expansion: Query rewriting uses an LLM to transform the user's raw query into one or more better-formed retrieval queries before searching - expanding an ambiguous or conversational query into explicit terms, breaking a compound question into sub-queries, or rephrasing to better match the document corpus's vocabulary. Add it when you observe retrieval failing on real user queries that are vague, contain pronouns referring to earlier conversation turns, or use different terminology than the source documents - it adds latency and an extra LLM call, so it's worth the cost only when retrieval quality genuinely benefits from it.
How would you evaluate whether a RAG sys: Use a faithfulness/groundedness check - either an LLM-as-judge prompt specifically asking 'is every claim in this answer supported by the provided context?' scored against the actual retrieved chunks, or a more structured approach extracting individual claims from the answer and verifying each against the source text. This is a distinct evaluation dimension from answer correctness alone - an answer can be factually correct but not actually grounded in what was retrieved (the model used its own parametric knowledge instead), which is a real problem for auditability even if the specific answer happened to be right.
What is the \"lost in the middle\" probl: Research has repeatedly shown LLMs pay more attention to information at the very beginning and end of a long context window, with relevant information placed in the middle being more likely to be underweighted or missed - even when the model's stated context window is large enough to fit everything. This means simply retrieving many chunks and stuffing them all into context isn't a reliable substitute for good retrieval precision; it's often better to retrieve fewer, more relevant chunks (helped by reranking) and place the most important ones near the start or end of the context, rather than relying on the model to find a needle anywhere in a very long haystack.
How would you design a RAG system to cit: Tag each retrieved chunk with its source metadata (document name, section, URL) before it's added to the prompt, and instruct the model explicitly to attribute each claim to its source chunk (e.g. via inline citation markers like [1], [2]) - then map those markers back to the actual source metadata in the rendered UI so users can click through and verify. For higher reliability, do this attribution as a structured output requirement (the model returns claims paired with source chunk IDs) rather than trusting free-text citations, which models can occasionally fabricate or misattribute.
What is contextual/late-chunking, and ho: Naive fixed-size chunking splits a document into chunks independently, losing surrounding context - a chunk in the middle of a document might not make sense without knowing what section it's from. Contextual chunking prepends a short LLM-generated summary of the chunk's surrounding context to each chunk before embedding it, so the embedding captures more of the chunk's true meaning within the document. Late chunking (a related but distinct technique) embeds the entire document first with a long-context embedding model, then derives chunk-level embeddings from that full-document representation - preserving cross-chunk context in the embedding itself rather than losing it at chunking time.
How would you handle a RAG knowledge bas: Attach recency/version metadata to every ingested document and either filter retrieval to prefer the most recent version by default, or explicitly surface the conflict to the model (and the user) when multiple versions of a fact are retrieved, rather than silently picking one. For a knowledge base prone to staleness, build an automated pipeline flagging documents that haven't been updated past a review threshold, and consider deprecating/archiving clearly superseded documents out of the active retrieval index entirely rather than leaving them to compete with current information at retrieval time.
When would you choose long-context (stuf: Long-context makes sense for a small, bounded, relatively static corpus (a single large document, a specific codebase) where the entire relevant content reasonably fits in context and retrieval precision isn't the bottleneck - RAG's main advantage (retrieving only the most relevant slice from a much larger corpus) doesn't help if you'd want to include nearly everything anyway. The tradeoff is cost and latency - processing a much larger context on every single request is significantly more expensive and slower than RAG's targeted retrieval of a few relevant chunks, and the 'lost in the middle' effect means a huge context isn't even guaranteed to be more accurate than well-designed RAG.
How would you design access control in a: Tag every document/chunk in the vector index with the access-control metadata it should respect (which roles/teams/permissions can view it), and enforce that filter at retrieval time as part of the vector search query itself (a metadata filter, not a post-retrieval check) - so unauthorized content is never even returned to the LLM in the first place, let alone shown to the user. Doing the access check only after retrieval (filtering the LLM's response) is much riskier, since the unauthorized content still passed through the model and could leak into the generated answer even if the final filtering tries to catch it.
What is a reranker's role in a RAG pipel: Embedding similarity search is fast but approximate - it's optimized for retrieving a broad candidate set efficiently across a huge corpus, not for precisely ranking the true best matches, and cosine similarity in embedding space doesn't always correlate perfectly with actual relevance to a specific query. A reranker (typically a cross-encoder that jointly processes the query and each candidate chunk together, rather than comparing pre-computed independent embeddings) re-scores the top-k candidates from the initial retrieval with much higher precision, at the cost of being too slow to run against the entire corpus - the standard pattern is fast approximate retrieval for a broad candidate set, then a reranker to precisely select the final few chunks actually sent to the LLM.
How would you debug a RAG system that re: This points to a generation-stage problem, not a retrieval problem - check whether the relevant information is actually present in the specific chunk retrieved (sometimes the right document is retrieved but the specific needed detail is in a different chunk of that same document that wasn't retrieved), check the prompt's instructions for ambiguity (is the model being told clearly enough to answer only from the provided context), and check whether the context is too long/cluttered with irrelevant chunks that dilute the model's attention on the actually-relevant one (the 'lost in the middle' effect). Isolating this from a retrieval failure - by manually inspecting exactly what was in the prompt sent to the model for that query - is the necessary first debugging step.
How would you design RAG for structured/: For structured data, text-to-SQL (having the LLM generate a SQL query against the actual database schema, then executing it and returning real results) is generally more reliable than trying to embed and retrieve rows as if they were unstructured text, since it preserves exact aggregation/filtering semantics that embedding similarity can't reliably capture. A common production pattern routes a query to either a SQL-generation path or a document-RAG path based on intent classification, and for genuinely mixed questions (some structured, some unstructured), combines both - text-to-SQL for the precise numeric/filtering part, and document RAG for narrative/explanatory context around it.
What monitoring would you put on a produ: Track retrieval recall/precision against a maintained evaluation set on an ongoing basis (not just at launch), monitor for corpus drift (documents added/removed/changed that might affect what's retrievable), track the rate of 'no relevant results found' or low-similarity-score retrievals as a proxy for coverage gaps in the knowledge base, and sample production queries periodically for human or LLM-judge review of end-to-end answer quality - retrieval quality can silently degrade as the underlying corpus grows or shifts even if the pipeline code itself hasn't changed at all, which is why ongoing monitoring (not a one-time launch evaluation) is necessary.
